newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerians in Europe vote on draft constitution.
newsitem.headline: Algerians in Europe vote on draft constitution.

text.p: Algerians in Europe and Tunisia began voting on Saturday on a draft constitution banning political parties based on Islam, the official Algerian news agency APS said.

Back home, Algerian security forces were deploying large numbers of troops in the main cities after a reported threat by the country's most feared militant group to "strike the necks" of people who took part in the referendum inside Algeria on Thursday, residents said.
The Armed Islamic Group (GIA), blamed for massacres of villagers and other civilians in the past six weeks, warned voters to stay at home on referendum day.
"We will strike with force the neck of anyone who goes to vote," the GIA said in a statement sent to news organisations in France.
The Algerian government announced a ban on truck traffic across the country on Thursday in an attempt to pre-empt any rebel attacks with trucks laden with explosives.
Residents in Algiers said by telephone that army soldiers and security forces increased the number of roadblocks and patrols in and around main cities.
There are 735,034 expatriate Algerians eligible to vote, most of them living in France, Algerian Interior Minister Mustapha Ben Mansour told APS.
"Many nationals have voted early in the morning before going for work," Algerian general consul in Paris, Said Abdiche, told the agency.
Voters were also lining up to cast ballots in polling stations in Italy, Belguim and neighbouring Tunisia, APS said.

The voting abroad will continue until Thursday when the poll takes place in Algeria. The turnout of expatriate voters is closely watched by the Algerian government as well Algerian voters as a first indication of the mood of the people on the referendum.

In last year's presidential election, television images showing expatriates flooding polling stations in France had encouraged voters at home to turn up in large numbers in defiance to Moslem guerrilla death threats, officials said.
The draft, if approved by a plurality of the 16.4 million voters, will replace the 1989 constitution which ended one-party rule.

The text broadens the president's paramount powers but it limits him to two-five year terms. It guarantees for the first time since independence from France in 1962 the right to form opposition parties to compete for government.
But it bans politicians from using Islam, Arab and Berber languages, gender and regional differences as means to seek power.
Main secular opposition leaders oppose the referendum saying President Liamine Zeroual's move to amend the constitution aims to set up what they called an "institutional dictaroship".
About 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a huge lead.
